resources.string: Arabic letters
The 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet and how their shapes change within a word.
Short vowels
Fatḥa (a), kasra (i) and ḍamma (u): small marks above or below a letter.
Sukūn
A small mark on a letter, as in بۡ, meaning it has no vowel, so it closes the syllable.
Long vowels
Alif after fatḥa, wāw after ḍamma and yāʾ after kasra stretch the vowel to two counts (natural madd).
Tanwīn
A doubled vowel mark at the end of a word, read as the vowel followed by n: an, in, un.
Hamza
The catch in the throat (ء). It can stand alone or sit on an alif, wāw or yāʾ: أ إ ؤ ئ.
Tāʾ marbūṭa
The round tāʾ (ة) at the end of a word: read as t when continuing and as h when stopping.
Shadda
A mark that doubles a letter, as in بّ: the first one has a sukūn and the second one carries the vowel.
Dagger alif
A small alif written above a letter, as in مَٰ. It is read as a long ā.
Small wāw and yāʾ
A small wāw or yāʾ that shows a long vowel the spelling leaves out, as in بِهِۦ (bihī).
Hamzat al-waṣl
The alif with a small ṣād (ٱ). It is pronounced only when you start reading from this word, and silent when joined to the word before.
Silent letters
A small circle marks a letter that is written but never pronounced, like the final alif in كَفَرُواْ.
Stop signs
Small signs above the text, such as ج‎, صلى‎ and قلى‎, that tell you where stopping is allowed, better or required.
Prostration sign
The ۩ sign marks a place where the prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwa) is made.
Empty space (al-jawf)
The long vowels ā, ū and ī have no fixed place: they flow from the empty space of the mouth and throat.
Throat letters (al-ḥalq)
Six letters are made in the throat: ء ه deepest, ع ح in the middle, غ خ nearest the mouth.
Tongue letters (al-lisān)
Eighteen letters are made where the tongue meets the roof of the mouth, the gums or the teeth, from ق at the back to ث at the tip.
Lip letters (ash-shafatān)
ب م و are made with both lips, and ف with the lower lip and the upper teeth.
The nose (al-khayshūm)
The humming ghunnah of noon and meem comes from the nose: pinch it and the sound stops.
Whispered and voiced (hams, jahr)
Ten letters are whispered, with some breath flowing out: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت. The rest are voiced.
Strong, middle and soft (shidda, tawassuṭ, rakhāwa)
Strong letters stop the sound completely, middle letters let it half through, and soft letters let it run on.
Raised and lowered (istiʿlāʾ, istifāl)
In seven letters the back of the tongue rises, which is what makes them heavy: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ.
Closed (iṭbāq)
In ص ض ط ظ the tongue presses up against the roof of the mouth and closes the sound in: the heaviest letters.
Whistling (ṣafīr)
ص س ز whistle: the air hisses through the gap between the tongue and the front teeth.
Rolling and leaning (takrīr, inḥirāf)
ر is ready to roll, so it is tapped once; ل and ر lean the sound to the side of the tongue.
Spreading and lengthening (tafashshī, istiṭāla)
The air spreads through the mouth in ش, and ض runs along the side of the tongue from back to front.
Heavy letters (tafkhīm)
Seven letters, خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ, are always pronounced with a full, heavy sound.
Lām shamsiyya (sun letters)
In ال before a sun letter, the lām is silent and the next letter is doubled: ٱلشَّمۡسِ (ash-shams).
Lām qamariyya (moon letters)
In ال before a moon letter, the lām is pronounced with a sukūn: ٱلۡقَمَرِ (al-qamar).
The lām in the name Allāh
The lām of ٱللَّه is heavy after a or u, and light after i, as in بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ.
Ghunnah
A nasal sound held for two counts on a noon or meem with shadda (نّ مّ).
Qalqalah
The letters ق ط ب ج د make a slight bounce when they have a sukūn or when you stop on them.
Noon sākinah and tanwīn
A noon without a vowel, and the n sound of tanwīn, is pronounced in one of four ways depending on the next letter. Idghām comes in two kinds: with and without ghunnah.
Iẓhār (clear)
Before a throat letter (ء ه ع ح غ خ) the noon is pronounced clearly, with no extra nasal sound.
Idghām with ghunnah
Before ي ن م و the noon merges into the next letter with a nasal sound.
Idghām without ghunnah
Before ل or ر the noon merges completely into the next letter, with no nasal sound.
Iqlāb
Before ب the noon turns into a hidden meem, shown by a small meem above it: نۢ.
Ikhfāʾ (hiding)
Before the other 15 letters the noon is hidden: between clear and merged, with a nasal sound.
Meem sākinah
A meem without a vowel is pronounced in one of three ways depending on the next letter.
Iẓhār shafawī
Before any letter except ب and م, the meem is pronounced clearly.
Idghām shafawī
A meem followed by another meem: the two merge into one doubled meem with a nasal sound.
Ikhfāʾ shafawī
Before ب the meem is hidden, with the lips lightly closed and a nasal sound.
Madd sign
The wavy line over a long vowel, as in آ, means: stretch it longer than the natural two counts.
Madd muttaṣil (connected)
A long vowel followed by a hamza in the same word is stretched 4 to 5 counts.
Madd munfaṣil (separated)
A long vowel at the end of a word, with a hamza at the start of the next word, is usually stretched 4 to 5 counts.
Madd lāzim (necessary)
A long vowel followed by a shadda or a fixed sukūn is always stretched 6 counts.
Rāʾ: heavy or light
The letter ر is sometimes heavy and sometimes light. Its own vowel decides, or, when it has no vowel, the vowel before it.
Heavy rāʾ (tafkhīm)
ر is heavy with a fatḥa or ḍamma, or with a sukūn after one: رَبِّ, مَرۡيَمَ, وَٱنۡحَرۡ.
Light rāʾ (tarqīq)
ر is light with a kasra, or with a sukūn after one: رِزۡقٗا, فِرۡعَوۡنَ.
Idghām of the same letter (mutamāthilayn)
A letter without a vowel merges into the same letter after it, said once, doubled: ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ, قُل لَّكُمۡ.
Idghām of letters from one place (mutajānisayn)
Two different letters made in the same place merge: قَد تَّبَيَّنَ, قَالَت طَّآئِفَةٞ. ط before ت keeps its heaviness: بَسَطتَ.
Idghām of letters from close places (mutaqāribayn)
ل merges into ر, and ق into ك, because they are made close together: بَل رَّفَعَهُ, نَخۡلُقكُّم.
Lām sākinah outside ال
A lām with sukūn in a verb, a particle or a noun (قُلۡ, هَلۡ, جَعَلۡنَا) is always pronounced, unlike the lām of ال. Before ل or ر it merges: قُل رَّبِّ.
Tanwīn before hamzat al-waṣl
When tanwīn meets a word starting with ٱ, its n takes a kasra to join them: خَيۡرًا ٱلۡوَصِيَّةُ is khayrani l-waṣiyyah.
Stopping on a word
When you stop, the last vowel drops, -an becomes ā, and ة becomes h: ٱلۡفَجۡرِ is al-fajr, كَبِيرٗا is kabīrā, رَحۡمَةٌ is raḥmah.
Madd ʿāriḍ (when stopping)
Stopping after a long vowel makes the last letter silent, so the vowel may be stretched 2, 4 or 6 counts: نَسۡتَعِينُ, ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ.
Madd līn (when stopping)
A wāw or yāʾ with sukūn after a fatḥa, just before the last letter, may be stretched when you stop: ٱلۡبَيۡتِ, خَوۡفٍ.
Madd ʿiwaḍ (when stopping)
Stopping on tanwīn fatḥ, -an becomes a two-count ā: أَفۡوَاجٗا is afwājā.
Madd badal
A hamza followed by its long vowel is stretched two counts: ءَامَنُواْ, إِيمَٰن, أُوتُواْ.
Madd ṣila, small and big
The hāʾ of “him” between two vowels is lengthened, shown by a small wāw or yāʾ: لَهُۥ, بِهِۦ. Before a hamza it is stretched 4 or 5 counts.
